etymology: From the Saxon hwaer, where, and fore, for — literally “for which cause.” In the Authorized Version it renders the Hebrew lakhen and maddua, and the Greek dio, hothen, and dia touto: sometimes asking why, far more often declaring therefore.
biblical_def: Wherefore is the hinge-word of Scripture, and it works in two directions. Interrogatively it demands a reason: “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2) — a question that indicts the whole trade of the natural man, who pays dearly for what cannot feed him. Far more frequently it is illative, drawing a conclusion out of what God has just said or done. This is its glory. The doctrine of Scripture is never left as bare information; it is fastened to the conscience by a wherefore. Because Christ humbled Himself unto death, “Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him” (Php 2:9) — the exaltation is not arbitrary, it is the Father’s answer to the obedience of the Son. Because our High Priest ever liveth, “Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost” (Heb 7:25): the security of the saints is deduced, not merely asserted. Because the engrafted word is able to save souls, “Wherefore lay apart all filthiness” (Jas 1:21). Mark the pattern — indicative first, imperative after; what God has done, then what the believer must do. The Authorized Version’s wherefore is the grammar of gospel logic, and to skip it is to sever duty from grace and leave a man with commands he has no power to keep.
webster_summary: For which reason; for what reason; therefore. In Scripture chiefly the illative particle by which a duty is drawn out of a doctrine already declared.
webster_full: WHEREFORE, adv. For which reason. Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.
For what reason; why: as, wherefore did Sarah laugh? (Gen 18:13).
From where and fore; Saxon hwaer and fore.
In argument, the particle introducing the conclusion of a premise.
Scripturally, the joint at which the indicative of grace becomes the imperative of obedience (Jas 1:21).
scriptures: Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Php 2:9
Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:
Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
corruption_summary: Modern versions frequently dissolve the AV’s connective particles into sentence breaks, and modern preaching follows — doctrine is announced in one paragraph and duty demanded in another, with the logical joint between them quietly removed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The loss here is not a redefinition but an amputation. When a translation or a sermon drops the connective, the hearer receives two disconnected things: a doctrine he is told to admire, and a command he is told to obey. He is never shown that the second grows out of the first. The result is the oldest error in practical religion — law without gospel, imperative without indicative — and it breeds either despair in the tender or self-righteousness in the hard. The Apostle never preaches that way. Romans spends eleven chapters on what God has done and opens the twelfth with I beseech you therefore. Ephesians spends three chapters on election, redemption, and adoption before the fourth says walk worthy. Strike the hinge and both halves fall.

Recover the plain sense: read every wherefore and therefore as an instruction to look backward before going forward. Ask what has just been said of God, of Christ, of the covenant — and then receive the duty as the fruit of it. This is not a grammatical nicety; it is the whole method by which the Spirit moves a doctrine from the understanding into the life. A believer who reads his Bible for its wherefores will never be able to separate believing from obeying, and will never be tempted to think obedience earns what grace has already given.
roots_summary: Saxon “for which”; in Scripture the illative particle fastening obedience to accomplished grace.
roots_lines: Wherefore — Saxon hwaer (where) + fore (for), “for which cause.”
Hebrew lakhen, therefore (Isa 55:2 uses the interrogative lammah).
Greek dio and dia touto, the standard illative particles of the Epistles (Php 2:9).
Interrogative sense: for what cause? (Gen 18:13; Exo 5:4).
Illative sense: the joint between doctrine and duty (Heb 7:25; Jas 1:21).
usage: Never read past a wherefore — it points back to the ground of the command that follows.
Php 2:9 shows the word doing doctrinal work: exaltation follows humiliation by the Father’s reckoning.
Isa 55:2 uses it to indict: the sinner’s spending is exposed by a single question.

etymology: Saxon hwider, to what place; the motion-word answering to where. It renders the Hebrew anah and the Greek pou with a verb of going — never where a thing rests, always where it is bound.
biblical_def: Whither asks the destination, not the location, and Scripture uses it to press the one question a man is most anxious to avoid: where is this road going? The angel of the LORD puts it to a runaway slave woman in the wilderness — “whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?” (Gen 16:8) — and Hagar can answer the first half only. She knows what she is fleeing; she has no idea what she is fleeing toward. That is the condition of every sinner out of Christ. Ruth answers the question the other way, and her answer is a covenant: “whither thou goest, I will go” (Rut 1:16) — a Moabitess binding her destination to the people of God, which is faith in its plainest dress. Thomas confesses honest ignorance of it, “Lord, we know not whither thou goest” (Joh 14:5), and receives for answer not a map but a Person: I am the way. And Hebrews settles the believer’s whither forever — “Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus” (Heb 6:20). The anchor is already inside the veil. The Christian is not asked to guess his destination; he is told that his Head has arrived there ahead of him and holds the place.
webster_summary: To what place; toward what end. The interrogative of destination, distinguished from where, which asks only of position.
webster_full: WHITHER, adv. To what place; used interrogatively: whither goest thou?
To what point, degree, or end; to what course of action.
To which place; used relatively: the place whither he went.
From Saxon hwider, of the same root with where and what.
Distinguished from where: where asks of rest, whither of motion (Joh 14:5).
scriptures: Gen 16:8
And he said, Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go? And she said, I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai.
Rut 1:16

And Ruth said, Intreat me not to leave thee, or to return from following after thee: for whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God:
Joh 14:5
Thomas saith unto him, Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?
Heb 6:20
Whither the forerunner is for us entered, even Jesus, made an high priest for ever after the order of Melchisedec.
corruption_summary: The collapse of whither into where is a small grammatical loss that mirrors a large spiritual one — an age content to describe its position and unwilling to name its destination.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply fallen out of use, and with it a distinction worth keeping. English now says where are you going, which is serviceable, but the older tongue had a separate word for the question because the question is separate. A man’s where is a fact; his whither is a judgment. The modern habit of speaking endlessly about where one is — one’s stage, one’s season, one’s process — while refusing to say where one is bound is not a neutral change of vocabulary. It is the native dialect of a generation that believes the journey has no terminus, and it leaves a man perpetually in motion and never on the way anywhere.

Recover the plain sense: Scripture insists that every road ends somewhere and that there are exactly two ends. The broad way leads to destruction and the narrow way to life, and the difference between them is not the sincerity of the traveller but the gate he entered. Ask the angel’s question of yourself as Hagar was made to hear it. To know whence without knowing whither is to be a fugitive; to say with Ruth whither thou goest, I will go is to be a pilgrim; and to know with the writer to the Hebrews that the Forerunner has entered already is to be an heir.
roots_summary: Saxon hwider, to what place — the question of destination, answered finally by the Forerunner within the veil.
roots_lines: Whither — Saxon hwider, to what place; the motion-form of where.
Hebrew anah, whither? (Gen 16:8).
Greek pou with verbs of going (Joh 14:5).
Answers the destination; whence answers the origin; where only the position.
Heb 6:20 settles the believer’s whither: where the Forerunner is entered.
usage: Gen 16:8 pairs whence and whither — Hagar can answer only the first.
Rut 1:16 is a confession of faith in the form of a destination.
Heb 6:20 makes the Christian’s destination a settled fact, not an aspiration.

etymology: Saxon hwanon, from what place; the origin-word answering to whither. It renders the Hebrew me-ayin and the Greek pothen, and asks after the source of a thing rather than its destination.
biblical_def: If whither asks where a man is bound, whence asks where he came from — and Scripture uses it to trace things back to their fountain. It is first a word of judgment: Adam is sent forth from the garden “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Gen 3:23), and the sentence is exact, for dust returns to dust and the man is put back to the soil that bore him. It becomes a word of faith when the psalmist lifts his eyes to the hills and asks “from whence cometh my help” (Psa 121:1) — the question is not despairing but leading, and the next verse answers it: My help cometh from the LORD. Not from the hills; from the God who made them. Our Lord uses the word to describe the sovereign freedom of the new birth: the wind bloweth where it listeth, “canst not tell whence it cometh” (Joh 3:8), so is every one that is born of the Spirit. Regeneration has a source, but not one the natural man can trace or trigger. And in glory the elder asks of the white-robed multitude, “whence came they?” (Rev 7:13) — and the answer is out of great tribulation, washed in the blood of the Lamb. Every whence in Scripture runs back at last to God.
webster_summary: From what place, source, or cause; from which. The interrogative of origin, answering to whither, the interrogative of destination.
webster_full: WHENCE, adv. From what place: whence comest thou?
From what source, origin, or premises: whence we may infer.
From which person or thing; used relatively.
Saxon hwanon, from the same root as where and what.
In Scripture, the word tracing effects back to their fountain (Psa 121:1–2).
scriptures: Gen 3:23
Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken.
A Song of degrees. I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help.
Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Rev 7:13
And one of the elders answered, saying unto me, What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?
corruption_summary: An age that will not ask whence must treat every blessing as an accident and every man as self-originated — which is precisely the doctrine of autonomy Scripture forbids.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live temptation is not that the word has been redefined but that the question has been abandoned. To ask whence is to confess dependence: help comes from somewhere outside me, life came from someone before me, the new birth has a source I did not supply. Modern man prefers to speak of himself as self-made, self-created, the author of his own story — and every such phrase is a refusal of Psa 121:1. The refusal is not intellectual but moral. A creature who traces his existence upward finds a Creator with claims on him; a creature who traces it nowhere keeps his independence and loses his footing.

Recover the plain sense: teach yourself to run every good thing backward. The help is real, and it came from the LORD which made heaven and earth. The faith is real, and it is the gift of God, not of works. The new birth is real, and it came like the wind — sovereign, unbidden, untraceable by the one born. Joh 3:8 is the death of every scheme that makes regeneration a thing a man does to himself or a preacher does to a crowd. The wind blows where it will. The right response to a mercy whose whence you cannot trace is not to claim it but to worship.
roots_summary: Saxon hwanon, from what place — the question of origin, which always terminates upon God.
roots_lines: Whence — Saxon hwanon, from what place.
Hebrew me-ayin, from where? (Psa 121:1).
Greek pothen, from what source (Joh 3:8; Rev 7:13).
Paired with whither in Gen 16:8 — origin and destination together.
Gen 3:23: the ground whence man was taken is the ground to which he returns.
usage: Psa 121:1 asks the question; Psa 121:2 answers it — never quote the first without the second.
Joh 3:8 makes the untraceable whence of the wind a figure of sovereign regeneration.
Rev 7:13 asks it of the redeemed, and the answer is the blood of the Lamb.

etymology: Saxon thanon, from that place; the demonstrative answering to the interrogative whence. It renders the Hebrew mi-sham, “from there,” and the Greek ekeithen.
biblical_def: Thence marks a departure point that God has fixed, and the word carries more theological weight than its four letters suggest. It is the word of the river that waters Eden and “from thence it was parted, and became into four heads” (Gen 2:10) — one source, four streams, the pattern of a blessing that divides without diminishing. It is the word of Babel, where the LORD scattered the builders abroad from thence, so that the place of man’s proudest gathering became the point of his dispersion. It is the word of gospel promise in the mouth of Moses: “if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart” (Deu 4:29) — and the thence there is exile, the far country, the very place of judgment. This is the astonishing thing: God names the place of chastisement as a place from which He may still be sought and found. And it is the word of solemn warning in our Lord’s mouth, “Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing” (Mat 5:26) — a prison whose thence has no exit, because the debt can never be discharged by the debtor. Two thences, then: one a place God bids you seek Him from, the other a place from which none returns.
webster_summary: From that place; from that time; for that reason. The demonstrative of origin, answering to the interrogative whence.
webster_full: THENCE, adv. From that place: he departed thence.
From that time; thenceforward.
For that reason; from that ground or premise.
Saxon thanon, from that; correlative to whence.
The redundant form from thence is idiomatic in the Authorized Version (Gen 2:10).
scriptures: Gen 2:10
And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads.
Gen 11:9
Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.
Deu 4:29
But if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul.
Mat 5:26
Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing.
corruption_summary: Deu 4:29 is regularly lifted out of its exile setting and preached as a promise that sincere seeking of any kind finds God — which reverses the covenant order and flatters the seeker.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is decontextualising. Deu 4:29 is quoted on posters and in devotionals as a general assurance that anyone who looks hard enough will find God, and the thence is quietly dropped. But the thence is the whole point: Moses is describing Israel scattered among the nations under covenant judgment for idolatry, and he promises that even from that place, if they seek with all the heart and all the soul, God will be found. It is a promise to a chastened covenant people, not a general law of religious effort. Strip the setting and it becomes a doctrine of works — seek sincerely, and God is obliged. Scripture never says that. It says no man seeks after God at all until God first seeks him, and the seeking that finds is itself the fruit of grace already at work.

Recover the plain sense: the promise is better than the counterfeit, not weaker. It says that no distance of exile puts a covenant child beyond recovery, that the place of discipline is not the place of abandonment, and that the God who scattered from Babel is the God who says seek me from thence. Set it beside Mat 5:26 and the mercy sharpens. There is a thence from which men are called back and a thence from which they never come out. The difference is not the earnestness of the prisoner but whether the debt has been paid by Another.
roots_summary: Saxon thanon, from that place — the fixed point of departure, whether of blessing, of scattering, or of return.
roots_lines: Thence — Saxon thanon, from that place; correlative of whence.
Hebrew mi-sham, from there (Gen 2:10; Deu 4:29).
Greek ekeithen, from that place (Mat 5:26).
From thence is the AV's settled idiom, redundant but emphatic.
Gen 11:9 makes Babel a thence of scattering; Deu 4:29 makes exile a thence of seeking.
usage: Gen 2:10: one river parted from thence — a source that divides without loss.
Deu 4:29 must be preached with its thence: it is a promise to the chastened, not a formula for the sincere.
Mat 5:26 names a place with no thence — no exit until an unpayable debt is paid.

etymology: The older singular form of always, from the Saxon ealne weg, “all the way,” hence through the whole course or distance. The Authorized Version keeps both forms; alway commonly renders the Greek pantote and pasas tas hemeras, “all the days.”
biblical_def: Alway is not merely often intensified; it is the word of unbroken continuance, and Scripture attaches it chiefly to God’s side of the covenant. The shewbread stands “before me alway” (Exo 25:30) — twelve loaves for twelve tribes, never absent from the table, because the people they represent are never off the mind of God. David is promised “a light alway” in Jerusalem (1Ki 11:36), a lamp that judgment itself will not extinguish, because the promise of a seed runs on to Christ. And the word receives its full weight in the last sentence of Matthew: “lo, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world” (Mat 28:20). The Greek is literally all the days — not a general benevolence hovering over the age, but every particular day of it, the dark ones included. The commission to disciple the nations would be intolerable on any lesser promise. Where the word is turned toward the believer it becomes duty: “Rejoice in the Lord alway” (Php 4:4), a command written by a prisoner, which proves it does not depend on circumstance. Note the order: God is with us all the days, therefore we may rejoice alway. The duty rests on the promise, never the reverse.
webster_summary: Perpetually; throughout the whole course of time; the older singular form of always, retained in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: ALWAY, ALWAYS, adv. Perpetually; throughout all time; as, God is always the same.
Continually; without variation or intermission.
From all and way; Saxon ealne weg, all the way, the whole distance.
The form alway is the older; both stand in the Authorized Version without difference of sense.
Rendering the Greek pantote, and in Mat 28:20 pasas tas hemeras, all the days.
scriptures: And thou shalt set upon the table shewbread before me alway.
And unto his son will I give one tribe, that David my servant may have a light alway before me in Jerusalem, the city which I have chosen me to put my name there.
Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, lo, I am with you alway , even unto the end of the world. Amen.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
corruption_summary: Php 4:4 is routinely preached as a demand for a cheerful temperament, and Mat 28:20 as a vague sense of divine presence — both readings detach the words from the objective facts that make them bearable.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is sentimental. Rejoice in the Lord alway is treated as an instruction to feel upbeat, which turns a command into a burden and a burden into a lie, since no one can manufacture a feeling on demand. The text does not say rejoice in your circumstances, nor rejoice in your progress; it says rejoice in the Lord, and it was written by a man in chains. The object of the rejoicing is unchanging, which is exactly why the rejoicing can be unbroken. Likewise I am with you alway is often reduced to a mood of comfort available to anyone feeling religious, when it is a specific promise made to a commissioned church engaged in a specific work — teaching and baptising the nations. Detach the promise from the commission and it becomes a pillow; keep them together and it becomes provision.

Recover the plain sense: alway means all the days, and the doctrine that upholds it is the immutability of God and the finished work of Christ. The shewbread was never taken away because the tribes were never forgotten; the lamp of David was never quenched because the covenant could not fail; and the Lord’s presence with His church admits no gap because it rests on His own oath and not on our consistency. Rejoice alway is possible only because He is with us alway. Put the promise first and the command becomes reasonable.
roots_summary: Saxon ealne weg, “all the way” — unbroken continuance, grounded in the unchangeableness of God.
roots_lines: Alway — Saxon ealne weg, all the way, the whole distance.
The older singular of always; both forms stand in the AV.
Greek pantote, at all times (Php 4:4).
Mat 28:20 has pasas tas hemeras — literally all the days, each one included.
Applied first to God’s faithfulness (Exo 25:30; 1Ki 11:36), then to the believer’s duty.
usage: Mat 28:20 reads literally all the days — the dark days are inside the promise, not exceptions to it.
Php 4:4 was written from prison; the object of joy is the Lord, not the circumstance.
The shewbread alway before God (Exo 25:30) pictures a people never off His mind.

etymology: The Authorized Version’s past tense of haste, from the Old French haste, speed, urgency. It renders the Hebrew mahar, to hurry, and chush, to make speed — the outward sign of an inward reckoning that the matter will not wait.
biblical_def: Scripture is careful about who hasted and why, for haste is a moral index. Abraham, seeing three strangers at his tent door, “hasted to dress it” (Gen 18:7) — the hospitality of a man who reckons the guest more urgent than his own ease. Rebekah at the well “hasted, and let down her pitcher” (Gen 24:18) and again “hasted, and emptied her pitcher into the trough” (Gen 24:20), and this readiness to serve a stranger and water his camels is the very sign the servant had asked God to give. The bride of Isaac is identified by her speed in serving. Against these stands another haste altogether: “Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered” (Est 6:12) — the hurry of a proud man fleeing a humiliation he cannot undo. And the taskmasters hasted the people (Exo 5:13), which is haste imposed by tyranny, the driver’s whip rather than the servant’s love. The lesson is plain enough. Haste is not a virtue in itself; it takes its character from its object. To be swift in duty and slow to wrath is godliness; to be swift in sin and slow in mercy is the mark of a corrupt heart. What a man hurries toward tells you what he loves.
webster_summary: Made haste; hurried; moved or acted with speed. In Scripture, the outward evidence of what a man reckons urgent, and so a test of his affections.
webster_full: HASTE, v.i. To move with speed or celerity; to hurry.
HASTED, pp. and past tense of haste, the AV’s regular form.
To urge or drive forward with speed; as, the taskmasters hasted them (Exo 5:13).
From the Old French haste; allied to the Saxon haest, violence, vehemence.
Rendering the Hebrew mahar, to hurry, and chush, to make speed.
scriptures: Gen 18:7
And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it.
And she said, Drink, my lord: and she hasted, and let down her pitcher upon her hand, and gave him drink.
Exo 5:13
And the taskmasters hasted them, saying, Fulfil your works, your daily tasks, as when there was straw.
Est 6:12
And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered.
corruption_summary: Our age treats speed itself as a virtue and slowness as a defect, which inverts the biblical rule — Scripture commends haste in duty and mercy, and condemns haste in judgment, in speech, and in the getting of wealth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the worship of velocity. Modern life measures a man by his output per hour and calls hurry productivity, so that a settled, unhurried spirit looks like laziness and a frantic one looks like diligence. Scripture makes a sharper distinction. It commands haste toward obedience — I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments — and toward mercy, as Abraham and Rebekah show. But it forbids haste in exactly the places the modern world demands it: he that is hasty of spirit exalteth folly, he that hasteth to be rich shall not be innocent, and he that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him. The world has the categories precisely reversed. It hurries into judgment, into speech, into debt, and into wealth, and then complains of exhaustion.

Recover the plain sense: ask not how fast but toward what. Abraham ran to the herd for a stranger; Rebekah ran to the trough for a servant’s camels; Haman ran home to hide his face. The same speed serves love in one man and pride in another. Cultivate the haste of Gen 18:7 — swift to feed, to serve, to forgive, to obey — and cultivate the slowness the Apostle James commands, slow to speak and slow to wrath. A Christian who is quick where God bids him be quick and slow where God bids him be slow will look strange to the age and will keep his soul.
roots_summary: Old French haste, speed — the outward measure of what a man counts urgent, and therefore of what he loves.
roots_lines: Hasted — AV past tense of haste; Old French haste, urgency.
Hebrew mahar, to hurry (Gen 18:7; Gen 24:18).
Transitive sense: to drive another with speed (Exo 5:13, the taskmasters).
Commended toward duty and mercy; condemned toward wrath, speech, and riches.
Rebekah’s haste is the sign by which the bride is identified (Gen 24:18–20).
usage: Gen 24:18–20: Rebekah is marked out as the chosen bride by her readiness to serve.
Exo 5:13 shows haste imposed by tyranny — the driver’s haste, not the servant’s.
Est 6:12: Haman’s haste is flight from shame, the exact opposite of Abraham’s.

etymology: From the Saxon witan, to know (whence wit, wot, wist), with the negative prefix — literally “not knowingly.” It renders the Hebrew bishgagah, in error or inadvertence, the standing legal term for sin committed without deliberate intent.
biblical_def: Unwittingly is one of the most searching words in the law, because it establishes that ignorance reduces guilt without abolishing it. If a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly, he must still restore it, and add the fifth part, and bring it to the priest (Lev 22:14) — the sin was unintentional, and there is still restitution and a sacrifice. The whole apparatus of the sin offering exists for exactly this class of transgression. The manslayer “that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly” may flee to the city of refuge (Josh 20:3), and there the mercy is real: he is not delivered into the hand of the avenger of blood, because he “smote his neighbour unwittingly” (Josh 20:5). But mark the limit of that mercy — he must run, and he must stay, and he is not free until the death of the high priest. Even innocent-of-intent blood confines a man to the refuge until a priest dies. This is the gospel written in the law: the unwitting sinner is not therefore a guiltless sinner, and his liberty waits upon the death of his High Priest. Our Lord’s own prayer stands over the whole doctrine — “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luk 23:34). Not knowing did not make them innocent. It made them candidates for pardon.
webster_summary: Without knowledge or intention; inadvertently. In the law, the term marking sin done in error, which still requires atonement and restitution.
webster_full: UNWITTINGLY, adv. Without knowledge; without design or intention; inadvertently.
From un and witting, the participle of the obsolete verb wit, to know; Saxon witan.
Of the same family as wot, wist, and wit, all signifying knowledge.
In the Mosaic law, equivalent to the Hebrew bishgagah, in error (Lev 4:2; Lev 22:14).
Distinguished from sin committed presumptuously, or with a high hand (Num 15:30), for which no offering was appointed.
scriptures: And if a man eat of the holy thing unwittingly, then he shall put the fifth part thereof unto it, and shall give it unto the priest with the holy thing.
Josh 20:3
That the slayer that killeth any person unawares and unwittingly may flee thither: and they shall be your refuge from the avenger of blood.
Josh 20:5
And if the avenger of blood pursue after him, then they shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand; because he smote his neighbour unwittingly , and hated him not beforetime .
Then said Jesus, Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do. And they parted his raiment, and cast lots.
corruption_summary: The modern rule that sincerity excuses — that no one is culpable for what he did not intend — is precisely the doctrine the sin offering was instituted to refute.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the enthronement of intent. The age holds it self-evident that guilt attaches only to conscious malice: if a man did not mean it, he did not do it, and to hold him responsible is thought unjust. This makes conscience the measure of sin, and since a seared conscience feels least, the most hardened man becomes on this reckoning the most innocent. Scripture reasons the other way. The standard is the law of God, not the awareness of the sinner, and the sin offering exists because men constantly break a holy law without noticing. David prays to be cleansed from secret faults — faults secret from himself. If ignorance excused, the entire Levitical provision for sins of error would be a needless cruelty.

Recover the plain sense: the doctrine humbles and comforts at once. It humbles, because it means you are guilty of more than you can recall, and no examination of your own motives will ever certify you clean. It comforts, because God made public provision for exactly that guilt, and the provision was not a lower standard but a substitutionary death. The cities of refuge make the point unforgettably: real mercy, immediately available, freely given to the man who did not intend it — and full liberty only when the high priest dies. Christ is both the refuge the manslayer runs to and the priest whose death sets him free.
roots_summary: Saxon witan, to know, negated — sin in ignorance, which the law treats as real guilt requiring real atonement.
roots_lines: Unwittingly — un + witting, from Saxon witan, to know.
Kin to wot, wist, and wit, the AV's other survivals of the same root.
Hebrew bishgagah, in error — the sin-offering category (Lev 4:2).
Opposed to sin done presumptuously, with a high hand (Num 15:30).
The manslayer’s freedom waits upon the death of the high priest (Josh 20:6).
usage: Lev 22:14: unintentional trespass still requires restitution with a fifth part added.
Josh 20:3–5: real mercy for the unwitting, yet confinement until the high priest dies.
Luk 23:34 shows ignorance as a ground for pleading pardon, never as a proof of innocence.

etymology: From the Old French deceite, and that from the Latin decipere, to take in, to catch as in a snare — de, down, and capere, to take. It renders the Hebrew mirmah, fraud, and remiyyah, slackness or treachery.
biblical_def: To act deceitfully is to take a man as a hunter takes a bird — by a snare he cannot see. Scripture traces the sin through every department of life. In the family it appears at Shechem, where the sons of Jacob “answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully” (Gen 34:13), covering murder with the language of covenant and circumcision — religion itself made the bait. In business it is the false weight and the withheld wage, the thing “which he hath deceitfully gotten” (Lev 6:4), which the law requires be restored with a fifth part added. In worship it is the great disqualifier: he that shall ascend into the hill of the LORD is the man with clean hands and a pure heart, “who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully” (Psa 24:4). And most solemnly it appears in the ministry, where Paul disclaims “handling the word of God deceitfully” (2Co 4:2) — the phrase means adulterating it as a huckster waters wine, and the alternative he names is manifestation of the truth. Job cuts to the root when he asks the comforters, “will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?” (Job 13:7). Men will lie on God’s behalf and call it defending Him. He needs no such defenders.
webster_summary: In a manner intended to mislead; fraudulently; by snare or false appearance. Applied in Scripture to speech, to trade, to oaths, and above all to the handling of God’s word.
webster_full: DECEITFULLY, adv. In a deceitful manner; fraudulently; with intent to mislead.
From deceit; Old French deceite; Latin decipere, to ensnare, from de and capere, to take.
In trade, by false weights, false measures, or concealed defects (Lev 6:4).
In oath-taking, to swear with a reserved or contrary intention (Psa 24:4).
In teaching, to adulterate or corrupt a text for advantage (2Co 4:2).
scriptures: And the sons of Jacob answered Shechem and Hamor his father deceitfully, and said, because he had defiled Dinah their sister:
Job 13:7
Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?
Psa 24:4
He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
corruption_summary: Deceit has been rebranded as skill — spin, positioning, curation, managing the narrative — so that the same act which Scripture calls a snare is now taught as competence.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is euphemism. No one advertises deceit, so it travels under professional names: the advertisement positions, the spokesman frames, the applicant optimises his history, the believer curates the version of his life that others see. Each word grants permission to create an impression the speaker knows to be false while keeping every individual sentence technically defensible, and that is precisely the sin Scripture names. The Hebrew mirmah does not require a stated falsehood; it requires a snare. Jacob’s sons at Shechem told no outright lie — they proposed circumcision, a genuine covenant sign — and used it as a trap. The most dangerous deceit has always dressed in true statements and religious clothing.

Recover the plain sense: measure speech not by whether each clause can be defended but by what impression it was designed to leave. Psa 24:4 sets the standard at the sanctuary door — clean hands, a pure heart, and no oath sworn deceitfully — and 2Co 4:2 sets it in the pulpit, where the only lawful method is manifestation of the truth. Job 13:7 closes the last loophole, the pious lie told to protect God’s reputation. A cause that requires deceit to advance it is not His cause, and a man who will shade the truth for God will soon shade it for himself.
roots_summary: Latin decipere, to take in a snare — the sin of creating a false impression, whether by lie, by silence, or by true words falsely aimed.
roots_lines: Deceitfully — Latin de + capere, to take down, to ensnare.
Hebrew mirmah, fraud, treachery (Gen 34:13; Psa 24:4).
The image is the fowler’s snare, not merely the spoken lie.
2Co 4:2 opposes it to manifestation of the truth — the minister’s only method.
Job 13:7 forbids the pious falsehood told on God’s behalf.
usage: Gen 34:13: a true covenant sign used as bait — deceit needs no stated lie.
Psa 24:4 makes truthful swearing a condition of approach to God.
2Co 4:2 condemns adulterating the word as a huckster waters his wine.

etymology: From the Latin ad, to, and pertinere, to reach or belong — through the Old French apartenir. To belong to by right, office, or nature; not merely to be near a thing but to be rightfully of it.
biblical_def: Appertain is a word of rightful belonging, and Scripture uses it to draw hard lines around what is God’s and what is a man’s. When the earth opens under Korah it swallows the rebels “with all that appertain unto them” (Num 16:30), and the following verses repeat it — their houses, their men, all their goods went down with them. Rebellion drags down everything that belongs to the rebel; a man’s household shares the fate of his defiance. The word’s greatest use is in Jeremiah’s doxology: “Who would not fear thee, O King of nations? for to thee doth it appertain” (Jer 10:7). Fear belongs to God as a debt belongs to a creditor. Reverence is not a temperament some worshippers happen to have; it is His by right, and to withhold it is not merely to be casual but to be in arrears. And the word draws the sharpest line of all at the temple altar, where the priests withstand king Uzziah: “It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests” (2Ch 26:18). A crowned and successful king is told that an office does not belong to him, and the leprosy that rises in his forehead settles the argument. What appertains to God’s appointed order cannot be annexed by greatness, sincerity, or success.
webster_summary: To belong, whether by right, by nature, or by appointment; to pertain to as one’s proper possession or office.
webster_full: APPERTAIN, v.i. To belong, whether by right, nature, or appointment.
From the Latin ad and pertinere, to reach to, to belong; French appartenir.
To be the property or possession of: all that appertained unto Korah (Num 16:32).
To be the office or prerogative of: it appertaineth not unto thee to burn incense (2Ch 26:18).
To be due as a debt or right: to thee doth it appertain (Jer 10:7).
scriptures: But if the LORD make a new thing, and the earth open her mouth, and swallow them up, with all that appertain unto them, and they go down quick into the pit; then ye shall understand that these men have provoked the LORD.
And the earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up, and their houses, and all the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods.
Jer 10:7
Who would not fear thee, O King of nations? for to thee doth it appertain: forasmuch as among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms, there is none like unto thee.

And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God.
corruption_summary: The age holds that any office may be occupied by anyone who feels called and competent, which is exactly the principle the priests refused to grant Uzziah at the altar.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the abolition of appointed order. Modern thought treats every office as an opportunity open to talent and desire: if a man is gifted, sincere, and effective, no further warrant is needed, and to tell him a thing does not appertain to him sounds like envy or gatekeeping. Scripture is immovable here. Uzziah was a genuinely great king, marvellously helped till he was strong, and his incense was offered in a real temple to the true God with what he no doubt considered devout intentions. None of it mattered. The office of burning incense appertained to the sons of Aaron, and his intrusion was not zeal but trespass. God has attached His blessing to the offices He has appointed and to no others, and gifting is not a commission.

Recover the plain sense: ask of any work not can I do this but does this appertain to me. The question restrains ambition and, just as importantly, it relieves the conscience — a great many burdens that crush Christians were never theirs to carry. The order runs both ways. Fear appertains to God, and He will not go without it; the altar appertains to His priests, and no king may seize it; and the ordinary duties of a man’s own station appertain to him, and no one else will discharge them. Korah wanted an office not his own and the ground took him; Uzziah wanted one not his own and the leprosy rose in his forehead while the censer was still in his hand.
roots_summary: Latin ad + pertinere, to belong by right — the word by which Scripture fences God’s honour and His appointed offices.
roots_lines: Appertain — Latin ad (to) + pertinere (to reach, belong).
Through Old French apartenir, to belong to.
Of possessions: all that appertained unto Korah went down with him (Num 16:32).
Of God’s due: fear appertains to Him as a right (Jer 10:7).
Of office: the altar appertains to the priests, not to the king (2Ch 26:18).
usage: Jer 10:7 makes reverence a debt owed, not a mood enjoyed.
2Ch 26:18 is the standing rebuke to gifted men who annex offices not given them.
Num 16:30–32: what appertains to a rebel is swallowed with him.

etymology: Saxon on sundran, apart, into separate parts — whence also sunder and sundry. In the Authorized Version it renders several Hebrew and Greek verbs of cleaving, parting, and breaking, always with the sense of a thing divided that was one.
biblical_def: Asunder always presupposes a union, and Scripture uses it to mark four kinds of parting. There is the parting God forbids: “What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder” (Mat 19:6) — our Lord’s word on marriage, which grounds the permanence of the bond not in the feelings of the couple nor in the law of the state but in the act of God who joined them. There is the parting God performs in judgment, as when the ground clave asunder under Korah (Num 16:31), and in glory, as when the chariot of fire parted Elijah and Elisha asunder (2Ki 2:11). There is the parting rebellious man attempts against God: “Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us” (Psa 2:3) — the nations raging against the LORD and His Anointed, straining at cords they take for bondage and which are in truth the only thing holding them back from ruin. And there is the parting the word of God accomplishes within a man: “piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit” (Heb 4:12), a blade that separates what no other instrument can distinguish and lays the thoughts and intents of the heart open. Note which unions God defends and which He divides. He fences the marriage bond and cleaves the self-deceived heart.
webster_summary: Apart; into parts; in a divided state. In Scripture, the word of separation — forbidden in marriage, executed in judgment, attempted in rebellion, and performed by the word within the soul.
webster_full: ASUNDER, adv. Apart; into parts; separately; in a divided state.
Saxon on sundran, apart; of the same root as sunder and sundry.
To cut, break, or cleave asunder, is to divide what was joined.
Of a bond dissolved: break their bands asunder (Psa 2:3).
Of discernment: the dividing asunder of soul and spirit (Heb 4:12).
scriptures: Psa 2:3
Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us.

And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Mat 19:6
Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.
Heb 4:12

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.
corruption_summary: Mat 19:6 is the single most widely disregarded sentence of our Lord in the modern church — marriage is treated as a contract the parties may dissolve at will, when Christ grounds it in an act of God that no man is competent to undo.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is the reduction of marriage to private contract. If the bond is merely an agreement between two adults, then it may plainly be ended by the same two adults, and the only questions left are procedural — how quickly, how cheaply, how amicably. Our Lord cuts that reasoning off at the root. He does not appeal to social utility, to the good of children, or even to the vows exchanged; He appeals to the act of God: what God hath joined together. The joining is His work, done at the wedding whether or not the couple knew it, and the prohibition follows necessarily — no man may put asunder what he did not join. The permanence is not a heavy expectation laid upon the couple’s endurance; it is a statement about who tied the knot.

Recover the plain sense: the same sentence that binds the married comforts them. A bond that rests on the act of God does not hang by the thread of present affection, and a Christian may therefore work at a hard marriage as a man works on a house he cannot be evicted from. Set Mat 19:6 beside Heb 4:12 and the pastoral order appears. God defends the union He made between husband and wife, and He divides the union a man has made between his flattering self-estimate and the truth. We commonly want it the other way — a searching word for our marriages and a gentle one for our hearts. Scripture gives the sword to the heart and the shield to the marriage.
roots_summary: Saxon on sundran, apart — separation, forbidden where God has joined and performed where God discerns.
roots_lines: Asunder — Saxon on sundran, apart, in separate parts.
Kin to sunder, sundry, and the German besonders.
Of judgment: the ground clave asunder beneath Korah (Num 16:31).
Of marriage: forbidden to man because the joining was God’s act (Mat 19:6).
Of the word: it divides soul and spirit, which no other blade can part (Heb 4:12).
usage: Mat 19:6 rests the permanence of marriage on God’s joining, not the couple’s resolve.
Psa 2:3: the cords the nations strain against are mercy, not bondage.
Heb 4:12 turns the word into a blade that divides what a man cannot divide in himself.
